Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control
I try to erase the memory of the event

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
The world is a dangerous place
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: For a 78-year-old woman whose index trauma is a natural disaster, this trigger is clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other triggers, appraisals, memory items, and strategies all fit disaster-related loss/danger themes, but 'being looked at sexually' implies a sexual-threat/sexual-trauma context that is not represented anywhere else in the formulation or item set. This is more than unusual; it introduces a qualitatively different trauma meaning network without supporting items in Threat, Memory, Appraisals, or Strategies.

vignette:
Margaret, a seventy-eight-year-old graphic designer who had spent decades creating order from visual chaos, could no longer sit still in her own home. The trouble had begun three years earlier, when Hurricane Cora tore through her coastal town and flooded the first floor of the house she had shared with her husband for forty-two years. She remembered the water rising past the kitchen counters, the sound of the back door slamming open and shut against the frame as the storm ripped it from its hinges. She had been alone at the time—her husband was at his sister’s—and she had stood on the second-floor landing, watching the brown water swallow her drafting table, her reference books, the framed prints she had collected over a lifetime. What frightened her most was not the water itself but the door: that rhythmic, violent banging, over and over, as if something were trying to get in. She had been certain she would die there, pinned by debris, and no one would find her until the water receded.

In the months that followed, Margaret did not speak much about the hurricane. She cleaned. She scrubbed the baseboards until the wood was raw, reorganised the pantry by height and colour, wiped down the same kitchen counter four times in an afternoon. It was the only thing that quieted the feeling that something was wrong, that the world was still off-balance, that she might walk into the living room and find the water creeping toward the sofa again. She also began to dwell on what she could have done differently: if she had boarded the door more securely, if she had driven to her sister-in-law’s earlier, if she had insisted her husband stay home. She turned these thoughts over like stones, hoping one of them might fit into the gap where her old sense of safety used to be.

The memories themselves were strange. Sometimes she could recall the hurricane in perfect detail—the smell of alcohol from a broken bottle of bourbon that had floated past her, the way the door banged—but she felt nothing, as if she were watching a film about someone else. At other times, the memory would seize her without warning: she would be standing at the grocery store and suddenly she was back on that landing, the water rising, the door slamming, her heart pounding as if it were happening right now. When she tried to tell her husband about it, the story came out fragmented, and she found herself thinking that it could not really have happened, that no one’s life could contain something so extreme. She began to avoid talking about the hurricane altogether, and when friends mentioned loved ones they had lost in the storm, she excused herself to the bathroom, her throat tight with an injustice she could not name.

At work, she had always taken pride in her precision. But now the sound of a door opening in the office hallway made her flinch so hard she often knocked her coffee cup over. She started arriving early to clean her desk, arranging her pens at perfect right angles, and she refused to attend meetings in the conference room nearest the emergency exit because the door there had a loose hinge that banged whenever someone entered. Her colleagues noticed her irritability, her sudden silences. One afternoon, a junior designer mentioned that her aunt had lost her home in a different hurricane, and Margaret stood up, walked out, and did not return for three days. She told her boss she had the flu.

What finally brought her to seek help was her husband’s quiet concern. He had found her on the floor of the bathroom, scrubbing the grout with a toothbrush at two in the morning, muttering that the door had to be fixed, that she could not let it happen again. She had looked up at him and for a moment did not recognise his face. That night, she agreed to call a therapist. She was terrified of what she might find—that the world was truly as dangerous as it now seemed, that the unfairness of what had happened would never be addressed—but she was more terrified of spending the rest of her life cleaning, waiting, and jumping at every sound.
